title: Arrays
summary: Keep a fixed row of values under one name, reach them by position, and loop over them safely.

steps.title: Many values, one name
body: Storing five scores in `score1` to `score5` is clumsy, and storing five hundred that way is impossible. An **array** holds a row of values of one type under a single name.
- `int[]` is the type: *array of int*. `string[]`, `double[]` and so on work the same way.
- Each slot has a position called its **index**. Indexes start at **0**, so the first item is `scores[0]`.
- `Length` is how many slots there are.
When you do not know the values yet, ask for empty slots:
int[] counts = new int[4];   // four slots, each holding 0
An array's size is fixed when it is created. It never grows or shrinks.

steps.explain: `n[0]` is 4 and `n[2]` is 15, so slot 1 becomes 19. Changing a value does not change how many slots there are.

steps.prompt: Complete the program. It makes an array with three slots, fills the first and the last, and prints how many slots there are.
steps.explain: Three slots have the indexes 0, 1 and 2. The last index is always one less than `Length`.

steps.title: Looping over an array
body: Arrays and loops were made for each other. There are two standard shapes.
`for` when you also need the **position**, or want to change the slots:
Start at `0` and continue while `i < pets.Length`. That visits every index exactly once.
A method can take an array as a parameter, like any other value: `int Sum(int[] numbers)`.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines so the program finds and prints the largest number in the array.
steps.explain: Assume the first item is the best so far, then let every item challenge it. This "best so far" pattern comes up constantly.

steps.title: Sum of an array
prompt: Write a method `int Sum(int[] numbers)` that returns the total of all the numbers in the array.
`Sum(new[] { 1, 2, 3 })` returns `6`. An empty array sums to `0`.
Write the loop yourself: the built-in `.Sum()` is off limits.
template: Dojo.Eq("Sum of an empty array is 0", 0, Sum(new int[0]));
hints: You want every value and do not care about positions, so `foreach` fits.
`foreach (int n in numbers)` and inside it `total += n;`

steps.title: Falling off the end
body: An array with 3 slots has the indexes 0, 1 and 2. There is no slot 3. Ask for it and the program stops with an **IndexOutOfRangeException**.
Console.WriteLine(a[a.Length]);  // the same mistake in disguise
The usual cause is the off-by-one error from the last module:
for (int i = 0; i <= a.Length; i++)   // <= runs one pass too many
Remember two facts and you will avoid most of these:
The crash is C# protecting you. Some languages quietly read whatever happens to sit next to the array in memory instead.

steps.prompt: After `int[] a = new int[5];`, which line crashes the program?
steps.explain: Five slots have the indexes 0 to 4. `a[4]` and `a[a.Length - 1]` are both the last slot. `a[5]` is one past the end.

steps.title: A broken average
prompt: `Average` should return the mean of the values in the array: `Average(new[] { 1, 2 })` is `1.5`.
It has **three** bugs. Two are in the loop header and make it crash. The third is quieter: the result loses its decimals. You may assume the array is never empty.
template: Dojo.Try("Average of { 2, 4, 6 } does not crash", () => Dojo.Eq("Average of { 2, 4, 6 } is 4", 4.0, Average(new[] { 2, 4, 6 })));
Dojo.Try("Average of { 1, 2 } does not crash", () => Dojo.Eq("Average of { 1, 2 } is 1.5", 1.5, Average(new[] { 1, 2 })));
Dojo.Try("Average of { 7 } does not crash", () => Dojo.Eq("Average of { 7 } is 7", 7.0, Average(new[] { 7 })));
Dojo.Try("Average of { 3, 4, 3 } does not crash", () => Dojo.Eq("Average of { 3, 4, 3 } is 3.333...", 10.0 / 3, Average(new[] { 3, 4, 3 })));
hints: Which index does the loop visit first, and which last? Compare with the valid indexes `0` to `Length - 1`.
The header should be `for (int i = 0; i < values.Length; i++)`.
An int divided by an int is an int: `3 / 2` is `1`. Make one side a double first: `(double)total / values.Length`.

steps.title: Counting from the end, and slices
body: The last item is `a[a.Length - 1]`. That is needed so often that C# has a shortcut: `^` counts **from the end**.
A **range** `start..end` copies a slice into a new array. The start is included, the end is **not**.
int[] first  = a[..2];    // { 10, 20 }      from the beginning
int[] rest   = a[2..];    // { 30, 40, 50 }  to the end
int[] tail   = a[^2..];   // { 40, 50 }      the last two
Leaving the end out is the same rule as `i < Length` in a loop. It also means `a[1..3]` has exactly `3 - 1 = 2` items.
Note that `^1` is the last item, not `^0`. `a[^0]` is one past the end and crashes.

steps.prompt: Given `int[] a = { 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 };`, match each expression to its value.

steps.title: Back to front
prompt: Write a method `int[] Reversed(int[] source)` that returns a **new** array holding the same items in the opposite order.
The `source` array itself must not change, and the built-in `Reverse` is off limits.
starter: // fill result so that its first item is the last item of source, and so on
template: Dojo.Eq("Reversed empty array is empty", new int[0], Reversed(new int[0]));
Dojo.Eq("the source array is left unchanged", new[] { 4, 5, 6, 8 }, dojoOriginal);
Dojo.Check("a new array is returned", !ReferenceEquals(dojoOriginal, dojoFlipped), "you returned the source array itself");

forbid.message: Does not call the built-in Reverse

hints: You need positions on both sides, so use a `for` loop over `i` from `0` to `source.Length - 1`.
When `i` is 0 you want the last item of `source`. When `i` is 1 you want the one before it.

steps.title: Sidekick piece: the week chart
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** `sk week` draws your week. Your `Sk.Bar(value, max, width)` from Control flow draws one bar, and `Sk.FormatMinutes(minutes)` from First steps writes `2h 10m`. Both are ready to call.
Write `static string WeekChart(int[] minutes)`. `minutes` holds one number per day, Monday first. Return one line per day (at most 7), joined with `"\n"`:

That is the day name from `{ "Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun" }`, a space, `Sk.Bar(minutes[i], max, 20)` where `max` is the **largest** value in the array, a space, and `Sk.FormatMinutes(minutes[i])`.

For `{ 60, 120, 0, 30, 0, 0, 0 }` the busiest day (120) gets a full bar of 20 `#`, Monday half of one. An array shorter than 7 gives only that many lines. `string.Join("\n", lines)` joins an array of lines.
template: Dojo.Eq("a week with a busy Tuesday", string.Join("\n", new[] {
Dojo.Eq("an empty week has 7 lines", 7, WeekChart(new int[7]).Split('\n').Length);
Dojo.Eq("an empty week has no #", false, WeekChart(new int[7]).Contains('#'));
Dojo.Eq("Sunday is the last line", "Sun #################### 3h 15m", WeekChart(new[] { 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 195 }).Split('\n')[6]);
internal static string Bar(int value, int max, int width)
hints: Find `max` first with a loop over the array (start at 0).
Make `string[] lines = new string[Math.Min(7, minutes.Length)];` and fill `lines[i]` in a `for` loop.
Each line: `$"{days[i]} {Sk.Bar(minutes[i], max, 20)} {Sk.FormatMinutes(minutes[i])}"`, then `return string.Join("\n", lines);`.
steps.explain: Two arrays walk side by side: `days[i]` and `minutes[i]` describe the same day. That is the classic use of an index.

build.title: The week chart
build.unlocks: `sk week` now draws your week as bars.
